paras: The Coal Hill convict camp killings were the deaths of Charles Williams, a Black convict, and other prisoners at a leased-convict coal-mining camp at Coal Hill, Johnson County, Arkansas, in early 1888. A coroner's jury found that Williams died from a whipping by the camp warden, J. A. Gafford, who fled, was indicted and was captured in Tennessee that November. The revelations led residents to threaten to hang the warden, prompted a state penitentiary board investigation, and were carried by papers across the country.

Coal Hill, near Fort Smith, was one of the Arkansas mining towns where the mines were worked with convicts leased from the state penitentiary. Gafford had been warden of the camp for about three months, succeeding a warden who had resigned.

According to the Arkansas Gazette account, Williams had been punished for not doing as much work as his partner, ran off and hid in the mines, and was brought out by a guard. On February 22 he was stripped, chained to the whipping post and given 400 lashes; that night he was taken to the hospital chained hand and foot, and he died the next day. The camp physician, Dr. W. Hunt, signed a certificate giving a congestive chill as the cause without seeing the body.

When Coroner Blythe's jury exhumed the body in March, it found the flesh whipped from the back, the right temple fractured and a large bruise over the kidneys from kicks. Its verdict was that Williams "came to his death from cruel treatment inflicted by J. A. Gafford, which consisted of whipping, violence and neglect." The St. Louis wire said Gafford hindered the inquiry and fled as the facts emerged, and the Memphis Appeal's Little Rock correspondent reported that he resigned and was believed to have gone to Memphis.

The inquest widened to other deaths. Witnesses said Gafford made prisoners fight, and a convict, Mose Harvey or Harney, died about March 8 or 9 after another convict, Mat or Marsh Bailey, kicked and beat him while the warden urged him on. The body of a white convict, Elder, was exhumed from a marsh with thirty-four gashes, and witnesses described a convict chained to a post and whipped to death the previous summer under an earlier warden. Ten or twelve new graves in the camp yard had no inquests, and convicts and guards were said to be afraid to testify.

Governor Hughes offered a $200 reward for Gafford's arrest and delivery to the Johnson county sheriff, and the penitentiary lessees, in whose employ he had been, added $200. A St. Louis wire said the people of Coal Hill were much excited and threatened to hang Grafford and tear down the prison barracks, and a later Post-Dispatch special predicted a "double lynching" of the warden and of George Crispi, a man jailed on a charge of assaulting a child. No lynching was reported.

On March 22 the governor and the penitentiary board went to Coal Hill, where they heard that the previous warden, J. B. Scott, had been even more brutal and that a colored convict, Frank Tellbert, had been shot in the mines on Scott's order. Physicians found convicts whom Gafford had whipped with bodies "almost solid sores." On March 26 the board reported that the lessees had broken its rules in nine particulars, ordered the chief warden dismissed and ordered the convicts returned to the penitentiary.

In November a Little Rock dispatch reported Gafford captured at Cumberland Gap, Tennessee, a fugitive since March and under indictment for murdering, or being accessory to the murder of, three convicts. Another former warden, J. A. Hugo, accused of beating a convict to death at the post, was arrested about the same time. Gafford was brought back in irons to the Johnson county jail to await trial, and no report of a trial or verdict appears in the coverage.

The story spread by wire from St. Louis on March 12 and 13 under headlines such as "Flogged to Death" and "Horrible Brutality," with one Minnesota headline placing it in Missouri. A Fort Smith version ran under the heading "Worse than Slavery," and a Kansas news column said prisoners had been "literally flayed alive." The reports gave the race of the victims, calling Williams a "negro convict" and noting that "colored convicts" had worked through the winter without shoes.

Arkansas papers turned the case against the convict lease system. The Yellville Mountain Echo called Gafford an "inhuman brute" and said the treatment was "the result of the penitentiary lease system," while the Nevada County Picayune ran the Gazette account under "Prison Reform Needed." The Memphis Appeal called the warden a "cruel brute" but described the convict question as beyond the state's capacity to solve. When Gafford was jailed in November, the Picayune remarked that "It will be no surprise if Judge Lynch gets in his work."

Accounts differ on Harvey's race: the early St. Louis and Fort Smith dispatches called him a white man of thirty-five, while the fuller inquest wire and the Gazette account called him a negro. A Post-Dispatch special of March 21 said the warden was in the sheriff's hands, but other reports that week and the November dispatch described him as a fugitive. One Arkansas paper said he had whipped four convicts to death, while the indictment concerned three.

reader.title: Coal Hill convict camp killings
bases: The deaths were attributed to a convict-camp warden and the punishments of the convict-lease camp at Coal Hill, not to a mob; Coal Hill residents only threatened to hang the warden (A2, A5, A11, A1).

Charles Williams was killed by a whipping that a coroner's jury blamed on warden J. A. Gafford, later indicted for murder, but the killing is attributed to one official exercising prison discipline, not to a group of three or more (A11, A5, A25); the threatened lynching of Gafford by Coal Hill residents was not reported carried out (A1, A12, A26).

A Little Rock special to the Memphis Appeal, the St. Louis wire, a Fort Smith dispatch and the Arkansas Gazette account agree that Williams was whipped to death at the Coal Hill camp and that the coroner's jury blamed Gafford (A2, A5, A9, A11).
